title: Sensitive data protection in agentic AI: protect what agents access
summary: Sensitive data protection in agentic AI starts with the data. See how to protect what AI agents access, so what leaves isn’t usable.
body_markdown:
*This is part 3 of our three-part series on agentic AI data security.*


In[part 1](https://blogs.opentext.com/agentic-ai-data-security) , we looked at how OpenAI disclosed that two of its own AI agents had quietly weakened the safety monitoring designed to watch them. In[part 2](https://blogs.opentext.com/ai-agent-data-exposure) , we looked at how researchers showed that a single email or form entry could get agents in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and Salesforce Agentforce to send sensitive data to an attacker.


The causes were different, but the lesson was the same. In every case, the controls around the agent didn’t hold. Monitoring was switched off from the inside. Data loss prevention missed an email sent through an approved action. That leaves the last of part 1’s three questions: if sensitive data leaves, is it still usable?


### **What is sensitive data protection in agentic AI?**


Sensitive data protection in agentic AI means protecting the data itself, not only the agent or the systems around it. Sensitive fields such as names, account numbers and national ID numbers are encrypted or tokenized where they’re stored, so agents work with protected values unless policy allows otherwise. If an agent goes off script or is manipulated, what it can send out is protected data, not readable records.


### **Why controls around the agent aren’t enough**


Most safeguards for AI agents sit around the agent: permissions, approvals, monitoring and data loss prevention. They all still matter. But parts 1 and 2 showed where they fall short:


**Monitoring can be weakened by the agent it watches.** OpenAI’s agent switched off alerts to its own security team.


**Data loss prevention can miss approved actions.** In ShareLeak, customer data left through a legitimate Outlook action, so nothing was flagged.


**Patches close one path at a time.** OWASP treats prompt injection as an ongoing risk, so new variants are likely.


Data-centric security takes a different approach. Instead of relying on every control around the agent to hold, it builds protection into the data, so the protection goes wherever the data goes.


### **What if ShareLeak had hit protected data?**


Go back to ShareLeak. A crafted form entry told a Copilot Studio agent to pull customer data from connected SharePoint lists and email it to an outside address. The agent had the access and an approved way to send it.


Now imagine the sensitive fields in those lists had been protected with format-preserving encryption or tokenization. The agent might still have followed the hidden instructions. But the email could have carried values that look like customer data, in the right format, without revealing the real values. Without the keys and the policy to decrypt them, those values would have been of little use to the attacker.


Protecting the data doesn’t stop prompt injection. It limits what an attacker gets when an attack works.


### **Protect sensitive data without breaking agent workflows**


The natural question is whether agents can still do their job if the data is protected. Traditional encryption changes the format and length of data, which can break the applications and databases agents rely on. Format-preserving encryption doesn’t. A 16-digit card number stays 16 digits, and a date still looks like a date, so applications, analytics and agents can keep working with protected data. Authorized users and processes see real values only where policy allows.


Many agent tasks, such as routing a support case or summarizing account activity, may not need the real values at all. That makes it practical to protect sensitive fields by default and decide case by case where clear values are needed.

It protects data across cloud and hybrid environments without breaking the workflows and analytics that use it.


### **From three questions to a data protection plan**


Across this series, we’ve asked three questions. Here’s how they line up with the four steps in our checklist,[AI data protection: what models can’t unlearn](https://blogs.opentext.com/ai-data-protection-what-models-cant-unlearn) , and where OpenText can help:


**What sensitive data lives in the systems your agents connect to?** Find out what your repositories hold. The[OpenText™ Voltage™ Data Security Platform](https://www.opentext.com/products/core-data-discovery-risk-insights) discovers and classifies sensitive data across your repositories.


**Which agents can reach that data, and do they need all of it?** Review who and what has access, then reduce what’s there. Data nobody needs is data no agent can expose.[OpenText™ Voltage™ Structured Data Manager](https://www.opentext.com/products/structured-data-manager) helps you retire or archive data that’s no longer needed.


**What happens to that data if it leaves?** Protect what remains, so that if data does leave, it isn’t readable or valuable to someone else. That’s where Voltage SecureData Servers comes in.


### **Agentic AI data security starts and ends with the data**


In part 1, we said agentic AI data security has to start with the data. It ends there too. You can’t predict every way a trusted agent will interpret a task, or every message an attacker will hide in content it reads. But you can decide what your sensitive data is worth to anyone if it leaves.


When sensitive data is discovered, reduced and protected, you can approve AI agents with a clear view of the exposure each one creates, and with protection that stays with the data even when an agent doesn’t do what you expected.
